paper.title_en: Where does the neutrino Mass Ordering preference come from?
paper.abstract_en: After the recent JUNO result, the comparison of the effective mass splittings measured in $\barν_e$ disappearance at reactors and in $ν_μ$ disappearance has become one of the leading handles on the neutrino mass ordering. In this paper, we study which data sets drive the present preference for the ordering, combining JUNO and Daya Bay with $ν_μ$ disappearance data from NOvA, T2K, MINOS, and IceCube/DeepCore. While the combination disfavors the inverted ordering at $1.9σ$, this preference comes from a balance between several small preferences. In particular, the combinations of reactor data with T2K or with NOvA point to opposite orderings. The values of the mass splitting preferred by these two experiments differ by about $3.5\%$, comparable to the difference expected between the two orderings, and thus a shift of this size in a single experiment is enough to reverse the preference. Moreover, in the context of this combination of reactor and $ν_μ$ disappearance data, further JUNO data would not bring the rejection of the inverted ordering beyond about $3σ$, as the comparison is then limited by the precision of the $ν_μ$ disappearance experiment. Improving the $ν_μ$ disappearance measurements requires control of the neutrino energy reconstruction, and thus the modeling of neutrino-nucleus interaction physics, at the percent level.
